figures.caption: Table 1. Prior work and the transfer question actually evaluated.

Figure 1: Task descriptions define the common output space. The 44 represented primary-training functional-task prototypes of the Bridge3 mixture, projected from 384 dimensions using t-SNE (cosine distance, perplexity 10, random initialization, seed 42). Each point is the normalized rich/canonical centroid for one task. Numbers identify the task names in Table S13. The original-space similarity matrix is shown in Figure S8.
Table 2. Frozen D2 source and class accounting.

Figure 2: Task labels and their source datasets. A filled cell indicates that a source contributes a task label. D1 has two multi-task datasets; D2 has five singleton-label datasets and two multi-condition datasets. The auditory-oddball and meditation/thinking datasets have shared investigator and facility provenance.
Table 3. All nine frozen conditions on D2: 8 s and K = 10.

Figure 3: Model rankings differ between development and reserved evaluation. Each point is a three-seed condition mean for eight-second inputs. D1 has been reaggregated using nonoverlapping windows and the same class–participant weighting as D2. Both candidate banks contain ten labels. The Spearman correlation across the nine condition means is 0.083.

Figure 4: All nine conditions on the reserved ten-class bank (D2). Circles show mean balanced accuracy with 95% intervals from 5,000 joint participant resamples, conditional on the fixed sources and three trained seeds. Crosses show the same means with one training-seed standard deviation. The vertical line marks 10% uniform chance. All inputs last eight seconds.
Figure 5: A small number of tasks account for most of the leading model’s balanced accuracy.

Figure 6: Distinguishing thinking from breath-counting meditation within the same EEG dataset. Exploratory two-class evaluation involving 98 participants. The model selected between thinking and meditation rather than between the ten tasks in the full D2 benchmark. Chance balanced accuracy was 50%. Circles and crosses indicate the participant-bootstrap intervals and training-seed standard deviations, respectively, as defined in Figure 4.

Figure 7: Distinguishing three driving conditions within the same EEG dataset. Exploratory three-class evaluation involving 18 participants. Candidate predictions were restricted to the three driving conditions, giving a chance balanced accuracy of 33.33%. Circles and crosses indicate the participant-bootstrap intervals and training-seed standard deviations, respectively, as defined in Figure 4.
Table 4. Training-data composition: task diversity versus repetition across studies.

Figure 8: Adding EEG datasets improves development performance unevenly. Balanced accuracy on the ten-task D1 development benchmark using eight-second EEG segments. Each point is the mean of three training seeds. The five training mixtures contain 0, 5, 10, 15, or 19 additional datasets, denoted SC0, SC5, SC10, SC15, and SCALL. Lines connect results obtained after the same number of optimizer updates. Although the fully expanded mixture outperformed the original mixture, intermediate additions did not produce monotonic improvements. The historical SCALL training recipe is distinct from the later ST19-MATCHED recipe.

Figure 9: Few-shot calibration substantially improves developmental task prediction, especially with examples from the same participant. Results for the historical full-addition model (SCALL), trained for 16,000 updates with seed 42, on the ten-task D1 development benchmark. Predictions use 64-second EEG queries, while support examples are labeled eight-second windows per available task class. Cross-participant support comes from one participant per target study, with other participants used for queries. Same-participant support comes from the queried participant’s own task recording, excluding any overlap in raw EEG samples. The zero-support reference is 26.50% for this seed; the corresponding three-seed mean is 28.98%. Chance balanced accuracy is 10%. Horizontal positions indicate support categories rather than a linear sample-count scale. The same-participant 64-window result is omitted because too few eligible queries remained.

Figure 10: Semantically related tasks are grouped more consistently with model predictions than source-matched random task groupings. Exploratory analysis of fixed-text Bridge3 LATE 64k on the combined 20-task D1+D2 benchmark. The original 20-class predictions are held fixed and evaluated after relabeling tasks into 15, 13, or 8 broader categories (F15, F13, and F8). Bars compare the observed semantic groupings with the mean accuracy across 10,000 randomized partitions. Source-conditioned partitions preserve both group size and the exact contribution of each recording source; size-only partitions preserve group size alone. The observed advantages over source-conditioned random groupings are 2.19, 4.18, and 3.91 percentage points for F15, F13, and F8, respectively.
